title: open-weight-selection-sales-guidance
content:
Executive summary:

This memo is a sales-facing guidance doc for positioning open-weight models and our "verified profiles" concept to customers and prospects. It is intentionally conversational and pragmatic — written for SDRs, AE technical champions, and solutions engineers who need quick, defensible answers when the conversation turns to reliability, safety, and selection criteria.

High-level thesis:
- Customers care about two things: predictable quality for their workload, and predictable unit economics. Open models are attractive for cost and flexibility, but the onus is on us to make selection and risk management simple.
- Instead of a single "verified" stamp, propose a small, operationally meaningful taxonomy (verification bands + evidence types) that maps directly to buyer decisions and deployment SLOs.

Suggested verification bands (language for sales):
- Band 1 — Field-validated: model variant that passed targeted workload evals, production canary at <customer-scale>, has rollback metrics observed. Use when latency and hallucination risk must be minimized.
- Band 2 — Benchmarked + curated: strong synthetic and unit-test performance on standard evals, plus quantization/latency profiles. Good for teams optimizing cost-performance tradeoffs.
- Band 3 — Community-sourced / experimental: newer open weights with limited vetting; low-cost option for rapid prototyping or non-customer-facing features.

Evidence types we surface (and how to talk about them):
- Behavioral evals (task-specific test suites) — "We run your prompt set or a representative corpus and show per-category metrics: exact-match, F1, hallucination rate."
- Stress profiles (latency and throughput at SLOs) — "We publish 95th/99th p50 token latency for your expected length distribution and batching."
- Regression history — "Model version X -> Y: we show diffs on key prompts and rollback plan."
- Deployment telemetry (canary outcomes) — "Canary at 5k requests/day for 72 hours with no quality regressions."

Sales cheat-sheet: when to recommend each band
- Startups/POCs: Band 3 to iterate quickly; emphasize low-cost experimentation and easy swap-in.
- Mid-market SaaS with user-facing flows: Band 2 as default; show curated metrics and latency bands.
- Enterprise / regulated: Band 1; combine private deployment option + Band 1 evidence (audit logs, canary results, KMS).

Short, defensible one-liners for pitches
- For cost-conscious teams: "Open models let you control inference economics — we make the selection predictable so you can optimize without sacrificing quality."
- For reliability-focused buyers: "We verify models against real workload tests and run safe canaries so your app keeps serving if a model update regresses."
- For compliance/enterprise: "Band 1 variants include deployment telemetry and integration options for private networks and key management."

Competitive landscape notes (quick read):
- Competitor A (managed closed models): simplifies trust via brand and SSO controls, but lacks transparency on model internals and has higher unit costs for large-volume customers. Our angle: lower unit cost + transparent evidence for customers who want control.
- Competitor B (open-hosting boutique): hosts many open weights but offers inconsistent vetting; sales often hit a trust gap — customer asks "how do I know this works for me?" Our verification bands directly answer that.
- Competitor C (self-host toolkits): great for infra teams but requires substantial ops investment to reach production readiness. Sell Redwood as the managed path that reduces ops while preserving choice.

Real objection scripts + rebuttals (short):
- Objection: "Open weights are risky — they hallucinate."
  Rebuttal: "Totally valid. That's why we run your canonical prompts as a smoke test and run Band 1 canaries that measure hallucination rate on your data before handing over production traffic."

- Objection: "We'd rather stick with the big closed model for SLA reasons."
  Rebuttal: "If SLA predictability is the blocker, our Dedicated + Band 1 pairing gets you predictable throughput and an explicit rollback plan — we can commit to latency targets and measurable quality gates."

Decision flow for solutions conversations (one-paragraph version):
- Gather SLOs (latency p95, token length distribution), failure tolerance (max hallucination rate), and cost targets. If latency or hallucination requirements are strict, propose Band 1 + private/dedicated deployment; if cost is the primary lever and tolerance for iteration is high, suggest Band 2 or 3 and propose a 2-week POC with tracked metrics.

Suggested customer-facing artifacts to unlock deals quickly:
- A 1-pager "How we verify open models" with three visual evidence buckets (behavioral evals, stress profiles, canary telemetry).
- A templated prompt-suite intake form for AEs to capture representative prompts and acceptance criteria during discovery.
- A quick-run canary kit (scripts + default dashboards) that solutions engineers can run in <48 hours>.

Experiments & metrics to validate messaging (prioritized):
1) Run 10 sales POCs where AE captures the customer's prompt set; measure time to first canary and conversion rate. Metric: conversion within 60 days.
2) A/B test two customer-facing one-pagers: "Verified banding" vs "single verified badge". Metric: win-rate lift in RFP responses.
3) Publish an anonymized case study showing Band 1 canary preventing a production quality regression. Metric: inbound interest and sales cycles shortened.

Notes / open questions (for product + research):
- How many evidence datapoints do customers need to feel comfortable? Is a short smoke test enough, or do teams insist on multi-week production traces? We should instrument this in early POCs.
- What language in legal / procurement will reduce procurement friction for customers that want to bring their own model weights? Get legal to draft a short clause.
- Operational cost modeling: what is the delta in SRE/SE effort to bring a Band 1 verification path for a new open weight? Needs input from infra/serving teams.

Next steps (who does what):
- Product marketing: draft the 1-pager and a templated prompt intake (owner: Lena Ortiz, due: 2026-01-20).
- Solutions eng: build the 48-hour canary kit and document the runbook (owner: Noah Kim, due: 2026-02-05).
- Research / Applied ML: pick 6 representative workloads and run them across 8 open weights to populate Band 2 baseline metrics (owner: Rishi Patel, due: 2026-02-28).

Quick TODOs in this doc (for author):
- Add link to the internal canary dashboards once Noah posts them.
- Formalize Band names if PM/legal requests stricter terminology.
- Get pitch lines verified with 2 AEs in EMEA to ensure phrasing translates.

Raw notes / brainstorming snippets (keep — this is a working doc):
- "Maybe offer a pay-for-verification add-on where we run customer dataset evals for a fixed fee"
- "Could we automate a 'confidence score' that maps directly to procurement categories? Eg. confidence 0-100 tied to allowed deployment modes."
- "If customers demand continuous verification, define an SLA for weekly regression scans and alerting."

End of doc.

-- Maya
